To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

perceived self-efficacies for positive affect regulation, negative affect regulation, empathic responding, academic performance, and resistance to delinquency are all positively related to each other, but only the latter two are also positively related to each others' behavioral outcomes, whereas the former three affect regulation self-efficacies are positively associated with the behavioral outcomes of the latter two self-efficacies.

self-efficacy to manage positive and negative emotions has an indirect effect on prosocial behavior and delinquency, whereas self-efficacy in empathic responding has an indirect effect in promoting prosocial behavior and in increasing the risk for depression.

the perceived self-efficacies for affect regulation and empathic responding are accompanied by the perceived self-efficiencies for academic achievement, prosocial behavior, and low involvement in deviant conduct, which in turn, contribute to positive psychosocial adjustment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how perceived self-efficacies for emotion regulation and empathic responding are related to diverse forms of psychosocial behavior and to the regulation of emotional distress.
affective self-regulation as an essential aspect of self-regulation in adolescence.
the role of affective self-efficacy in the regulation and development of psychosocial competence and vulnerability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

perceived self-efficacv for affect regulation has an indirect impact on psychosocial functioning, operating through the perceived self-efficacies for academic development, prosocial behavior, empathy, and delinquency.

perceived affective self-regulation is a critical factor in the development of adolescent psychosocial competence and well-being, and that its influence is channeled through the efficacy beliefs and competencies in diverse behavioral domains.
perceived self-efficacies to regulate affect and to manage behavioral domains are interwoven in their influence on psychosocial functioning in late adolescence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
affective self-efficacy is an important construct that operates as a generalized contributor in governing diverse spheres in psychosocial development.
perceived self-efficacies to regulate affect and to behave in prosocial ways are interrelated in their operation on adolescent psychosocial functioning.
affect regulation is a key to psychosocial competence in adolescence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
affect regulation is an integral part of psychosocial development.
affective self-regulation is an important component of psychosocial development.
perceived efficacy to regulate affect is a key factor in the developmental course of psychosocial adjustment.
